footer.scope: Robot Tuner is for differential-drive robots: two driven wheels, or four-wheel skid steer with the left and right pairs driven together, with 1 to 5 distance sensors. Wheel encoders are strongly recommended (without them the robot runs in a time-based mode and turns drift). Mecanum, omni-wheel and car-like (steering) robots are out of scope.
footer.offline: Runs in your browser. Works offline once loaded.
home.title: Home
home.h1: Get your robot driving straight down the middle of the corridor.
home.lead: Robot Tuner is for students building a small two-wheel robot that drives between two walls. You don't need to know PID yet: the site explains what you need, when you need it.
home.in_1: Differential drive: 2 driven wheels (plus a caster), or 4-wheel skid steer with the left pair and the right pair driven together.
home.in_2: Wheel encoders on the driven wheels: quadrature, single-channel (slotted disc) or AS5600. Without encoders only a time-based mode (turns drift).
home.in_3: 1 to 5 distance sensors (VL53L0X, VL53L1X, Sharp IR, HC-SR04, or your own values).
home.out_3: Fully encoder-free robots get only a limited, time-based calibration.
home.f_builder: Describe your robot: size, wheels and where each sensor looks. Everything else uses this.
home.f_measure: Measure the real robot: wheel ticks, speed, wheel spacing, sensor noise. With USB or by hand.
home.f_corridor: Set up the corridor to test in: width, wall errors, where the robot starts.
home.f_train: Press Start: the computer searches the best Kp, Ki, Kd and speed, then gives you C code.
home.f_playground: Try gains yourself while the robot drives, and compare them side by side.
home.f_troubleshoot: Your real robot wobbles, drifts or reacts late? Find the cause and what to change.
home.f_tutorial: What P, I and D each do, with small demos you can play with.
home.f_maze: Once the corridor works: test wall following, flood fill and mapping in realistic mazes.
home.how_1: The physics is the C++ simulator of the Simulation-To-Real-Life project, compiled to WebAssembly: distance sensors with their cone, noise, dropouts and reading age; wheel encoders; the firmware's own wheel-speed PID driving a DC-motor model; wheel slip and per-robot build errors. An automatic test checks that the browser gives exactly the same numbers as the C++ program.
builder.intro: Describe your robot as seen from above. The origin is the midpoint between the two driven wheels (the point the robot turns around): +x points forward, +y to the LEFT, angles are counter-clockwise. Everything you change is drawn at once and saved in this browser.
builder.name: Name
builder.drive_4wd: 4-wheel skid steer (left pair and right pair driven together)
builder.front: Front edge ahead of the axle
builder.origin_note: Measure from the axle (the line through both wheel centres) to the front and to the back of the body.
builder.skid_note: A skid-steer robot turns like a 2-wheel robot with a WIDER track: the wheels scrub sideways. The spin test in Measure gives the effective value.
builder.track_eff_note: What the robot really turns with (from the spin test). Starts equal to the wheel spacing; measure it in step 'Spin test'.
builder.caster_on: Has a caster ball (the free-rolling ball or wheel that holds up the front or back)
builder.caster_x: Caster position x (+ = ahead of the axle)
builder.sensors_intro: 1 to 5 distance sensors. For centring between two walls you need at least one sensor looking left (angle > 15°) and one looking right (angle < -15°). Drag a sensor on the drawing to move it; Shift + drag rotates it.
builder.step_tau_note: How long a wheel needs to reach 63 % of a new speed (step test). Used by the simple motor model.
builder.timing_note: Loop period = how often the robot decides (set by the sensor rate). Reading age = how old the distance is when it is used. You do not choose these, you measure them; what you choose is the speed.
builder.motor_model_note: The full model runs the firmware's wheel-speed PID on a fitted DC-motor model. If you did not fit a motor model, use the simple lag (it only needs top speed and response time).
builder.file_p: Your robot is one JSON file. Export it to keep it, share it or edit it later; import it on any computer.
builder.hw_p: robot_hardware.txt is the format of the Simulation-To-Real-Life project (tools/gen_hardware.py reads it). Sensor poses are written explicitly.
builder.confirm_new: Replace the current robot? Export it first if you want to keep it.
builder.canvas_hint: Drag: move view · wheel: zoom · drag a sensor: move it · Shift+drag: rotate it · Alt+drag: move the caster ball
builder.chk_noside: No sensor looks to the side: the robot cannot see the walls it must stay between.
builder.chk_oneside: Sensors look to one side only: use 'follow one wall' mode in the playground (centring needs both sides).
builder.chk_twoside: Left- and right-looking sensors present: centring with PID is possible.
builder.chk_wheels_out: The wheels stick out far beyond the body: they will touch the walls first.
builder.chk_track_eff: Effective track width differs from the wheel spacing by more than 25 %: re-check the spin test.
builder.chk_sensor_out: Sensor #{n} is outside the body outline. Intended?
builder.chk_wheelbase: Axle distance is smaller than the wheel diameter: the wheels would overlap.
builder.chk_range: A side sensor's maximum range is below 15 cm: in a wide corridor it will not see the wall.
builder.source_hint: Where the value comes from. N/A = not set yet (the drawing uses a placeholder). TYPED = you typed it, MEASURED = from the Measure page, IMPORTED = from a file, DATASHEET = from the sensor type.
sensor.note.VL53L0X: Laser time-of-flight, 25° diagonal field of view (18° horizontal), ~33 ms per reading by default.
sensor.note.VL53L1X_short: Laser time-of-flight, 27° diagonal (19° horizontal), short mode: up to 1.3 m, 20 ms budget, 25 ms period. Our robot's sensor.
sensor.note.VL53L1X_long: Laser time-of-flight, long mode: up to 4 m, but at least 33 ms per reading and more sensitive to ambient light.
sensor.note.GP2Y0A21: Analog infrared triangulation. Narrow beam, new value every ~39 ms, noise grows with distance; reads nonsense below 10 cm.
sensor.note.GP2Y0A41: Analog infrared, short range 4-30 cm, ~17 ms per reading.
sensor.note.HC_SR04: Ultrasonic echo, wide beam (~30°). No echo from walls hit at a shallow angle (> ~40° from head-on). Do not trigger faster than every 60 ms.
sensor.f.max_incidence_deg: Max angle to the wall for an echo (0 = any)
corr.intro: Build the corridor your robot must drive: an endless straight corridor with the errors of a real, hand-built one, or a track you draw. The robot uses your robot description and its current PID gains. These settings are also used by the playground and by training.
corr.track_note: The walls are the centre line moved half the width to each side; corners are rounded with the radius. .track files from the Simulation-To-Real-Life project (freeform format) can be imported.
corr.draw_help: Click to add a point, drag a point to move it, right-click (or Ctrl+click) a point to delete it. With "Closed loop" on, the last point joins the first.
corr.errors_note: Real corridors are not perfect. Switch each kind of error on or off and choose its size. Every corridor number gives a different, repeatable corridor.
corr.start_random: Random start (up to the angle above)
corr.start_adjusted_angle: The robot does not fit at this angle: started at {a}° instead.
corr.start_adjusted_offset: Offset reduced so the robot does not start inside a wall.
corr.start_impossible: The robot does not fit in this corridor at all.
corr.to_playground: Tune the gains in the playground →
err.jitter.hint: Small random unevenness along the walls.
err.tilt.hint: Each wall board (40-80 cm) is rotated by a small random angle.
err.bumps.hint: Short things sticking out of the wall (screws, tape, a misplaced board).
err.gaps.hint: Missing wall pieces: the side sensor suddenly sees far away.
err.steps.hint: One wall jumps in or out: the corridor gets wider or narrower.
noise.global_hint: 0 = perfect robot, 1 = like our real robot, 2 = twice as bad.
noise.mismatch_hint: One wheel slightly bigger / its motor stronger. The encoders cannot see it.
noise.delay_hint: Added to the measured reading age: the robot reacts to older data.
noise.angle_bias: Sensors glued on a few degrees off (random per run)
plot.center_err: Centring error (mm, + = left of the centre)
pg.intro: Change the gains while the robot drives and watch the path, the errors and the wheel commands. Try a preset to see a classic mistake, or run a sweep to compare several values side by side from exactly the same start.
pg.kp_hint: Turns harder the bigger the left-right difference is now.
pg.ki_hint: Slowly removes an error that stays (e.g. one weaker wheel).
pg.kd_hint: Brakes the turn when the error shrinks fast: less overshoot.
pg.units: Error = left distance − right distance (m), clipped. Turn = Kp·error + Ki·∫error + Kd·d(error)/dt (filtered), in m/s. Base = v_min + speed_frac·(v_max − v_min), constant. Right wheel = base + turn, left wheel = base − turn, each cut at ±v_max.
pg.save_gains: Save these gains to my robot
pg.sweep_p: Ghost robots start at the same pose with the same noise; only the chosen value differs.
preset.good.desc: Your robot with its current gains: the reference.
preset.p_low.desc: Kp far too small: the robot corrects so slowly that it drifts along off-centre and nearly touches the wall.
preset.p_high.desc: Kp far too big: every small error causes a big turn, the robot overshoots and wobbles left-right.
preset.no_d.desc: No derivative: nothing brakes the turn as the error shrinks, so the robot swings through the centre line before settling.
preset.i_windup.desc: A big Ki keeps adding up the error during the start manoeuvre; long after the robot is centred the stored integral still pushes it to the other side.
preset.too_fast.desc: A motor 4× faster than measured (Max wheel speed) at the same speed_frac, with old sensor data (150 ms extra delay): by the time it reacts it has already moved on. It reacts late and swings.
preset.saturation.desc: speed_frac 1.0: the cruise speed IS the top speed, so the outer wheel cannot go any faster and the turn the PID asks for is cut off (its wheel turns red). It cannot turn back in time.
preset.mismatch.desc: The right wheel is 8 % faster and Ki = 0: P alone leaves a steady offset from the centre. Add some Ki to remove it.
ts.h1: Troubleshooting: on the real robot it does X
ts.intro: Find what your real robot does, read why, try the suggestions one at a time, and open the simulation that reproduces it.
ts.wobble.why: Each small error causes a turn that is too big, so it overshoots the centre again and again.
ts.wobble.try: Lower Kp (halve it).|Raise Kd a little: it brakes the turn as the error shrinks.|Lower the speed.|Check that one sensor is not reading glitches (noise looks like error to P and especially to D).
ts.drift.sym: It drifts slowly to a wall and corrects too late
ts.drift.why: Kp is too small: the turn it asks for is too weak for the error.
ts.drift.try: Raise Kp (double it) until it starts to wobble, then go back a bit.|Check the sign: a wrong sign makes it steer TOWARD the wall.
ts.overshoot.sym: After a disturbance it swings through the centre before settling
ts.overshoot.why: Nothing brakes the turn while the error shrinks.
ts.overshoot.try: Add Kd (start with Kd ≈ Kp / 5).|Lower Kp slightly.
ts.late.sym: It reacts late, as if it saw the wall too late
ts.late.why: Between two decisions the robot moves speed × loop period, and the data is already old (reading age). At high speed that is a lot.
ts.late.try: Lower the speed.|Measure the loop period and reading age (Measure page) and put them in the robot: the sim then shows the real delay.|Make the loop faster: shorter sensor timing budget, no slow code (Serial prints, delay()) in the loop.
ts.cant_turn.sym: It cannot turn back at full speed
ts.cant_turn.why: One wheel is already at maximum: the turn it needs cannot be added, so it is cut off (saturation).
ts.cant_turn.try: Lower speed_frac (the default 0.75 leaves a quarter of the speed range to turn).|Watch the Clipping panel on the Playground: the red wheel is the one at its limit.
ts.one_side.sym: It always drives a bit off-centre to one side
ts.one_side.why: A constant error: one motor/wheel stronger than the other, or a sensor angle / bias not as you think.
ts.one_side.try: Check the sensor angles and mounting (both side sensors must look equally far forward).|Measure sensor bias (Measure → sensor test) and subtract it.|Add a small Ki to remove a steady offset.|Check the wheel mismatch with the straight drive test.
ts.swing_after.sym: Long after the start it still swings to the other side
ts.swing_after.why: Integral windup: the I term collected a big error during the start and needs a long time to unwind.
ts.swing_after.try: Lower Ki.|Limit the integral (anti-windup limit).|Reset the integral after a big manoeuvre.
ts.gaps.sym: It jerks at gaps or openings in the wall
ts.gaps.why: A gap makes one side sensor read far away: a huge sudden error.
ts.gaps.try: Clip the error (error limit) so one reading cannot command a violent turn.|Ignore sudden jumps of one sensor for a short time (glitch filter).|Turn on 'Gaps' in the corridor errors and test.
tr.intro: The computer drives your robot down straight corridors many times, every time starting rotated and off-centre, with real wall errors. It keeps the gains that get parallel and centred fastest and stay there without crashing. First a grid search over Kp, Ki, Kd (and the speed), then a genetic algorithm refines the best ones: the same method and reward as our research simulator. About 1-5 minutes.
tr.reporting: Testing the best gains at 0×, 1× and 2× noise…
tr.use: Use these gains for my robot
tr.plot_crash: Crash % of the best, per generation
tr.report_p: The best gains on new corridors and starts, with no noise, the noise you set, and twice that.
ms.intro: Connect the robot (USB, or Bluetooth for the steps where it drives) and let it measure itself, one step at a time. Each step says what it measures, why it matters and what to do. Results go into your robot description (marked MEASURED). No robot or other firmware? Type the values instead.
ms.nosupport: Your browser cannot talk to USB devices. Use Chrome or Edge on a computer, or type the values by hand (manual mode).
ms.manual_note: Every step also accepts typed values, e.g. from your own measurement program.
ms.nofw_h: No firmware that answers these commands?
ms.nofw_p: Robot builder → Firmware generates a sketch for your wiring (board, encoders, motor driver, sensors) that answers these commands. The file below is the sketch for the example robot (ESP32, DRV8833, quadrature encoders, 3× VL53L1X).
ms.connect_first: Connect the robot first, or use manual mode.
ms.type_note: Typed values are saved at once.
ms.physical.title: Measure the robot with a ruler
ms.physical.what: Body size, wheel diameter and width, wheel spacing, axle position, caster and the position and angle of every sensor.
ms.physical.why: The simulator needs the robot's shape to know when it touches a wall, and the sensor poses to know what each sensor sees.
ms.physical.how: Measure from the axle (the line through both wheel centres) in millimetres. Sensor angles: 0° = straight ahead, + = to the left.
ms.physical.p: Enter these in the robot builder; the drawing updates while you type.
ms.ticks.title: Encoder ticks per wheel turn
ms.ticks.what: How many encoder ticks one full wheel revolution gives.
ms.ticks.why: Every distance and speed the robot measures comes from this number.
ms.ticks.how: Motors are off. Put a pen mark on each tyre and line it up with something fixed. Press Start, then turn each wheel forward by hand, slowly, exactly one full turn (mark back at the start) and press the button; repeat for every turn. N turns divided by N is much more accurate than one turn.
ms.maxspeed.title: Top speed
ms.maxspeed.what: The wheel speed at full power.
ms.maxspeed.why: The PID cannot ask for more than this. Cruising close to it leaves no room to steer (saturation).
ms.maxspeed.how: Lift the robot so the wheels turn freely (wheels in the air!), with a full battery. Press Start: both wheels run at full power for one second.
ms.ff.title: Motor feed-forward and deadband
ms.ff.what: The PWM needed to start moving (deadband) and how much PWM each extra unit of speed needs.
ms.ff.why: The wheel speed controller uses these to reach a new speed quickly without waiting for its integral.
ms.ff.how: Wheels in the air. Press Start: the PWM rises step by step (about a minute).
ms.step.title: Wheel response time
ms.step.what: How long a wheel takes to reach a new speed (63 % of the step = time constant).
ms.step.why: This lag is part of every steering decision: the robot cannot turn faster than its wheels can change speed.
ms.step.how: Wheels in the air. Press Start: both wheels jump from 0 to a target speed and the response is recorded.
ms.drive.title: Straight drive
ms.drive.what: Whether 1 m on the encoders is really 1 m (wheel diameter error, left/right difference).
ms.drive.why: Wrong wheel scale = wrong speeds and distances; a left/right difference makes the robot curve.
ms.drive.how: Put the robot on the floor with 1.5 m free in front. Press Start: it drives 1 m by its encoders. Measure how far it really went.
ms.drive.ask: How far did the robot really drive? (metres, e.g. 0.985)
ms.spin.title: Effective track width
ms.spin.what: The wheel spacing the robot really turns with.
ms.spin.why: Turning depends on it. It is usually a bit larger than the measured wheel spacing (tyre contact, scrub); for 4-wheel skid steer much larger.
ms.spin.how: Floor, free space around. Stick a piece of tape on the floor under the robot's nose. Press Start: it spins N times in place by its encoders (default 10). Count the REAL turns as the nose passes the tape, with fractions (e.g. 9.8).
ms.spin.untrusted: The spin was not symmetric or the motors hit their limit: the result may be wrong. Lower the spin speed and repeat.
ms.tof.title: Sensor noise and bias
ms.tof.what: For each sensor: how much the reading jumps (noise), how far off it is on average (bias), how often it gives no reading.
ms.tof.why: Noise is what the D term amplifies; a bias makes the robot drive off-centre.
ms.tof.how: Put a flat board at a known distance in front of each sensor (e.g. 200 mm), robot not moving. Press Start: each sensor takes 200 readings.
ms.tof.ask: True distance from each sensor to its board (mm)
ms.timing.title: Loop period and reading age
ms.timing.what: Loop period = how often the robot decides. Reading age (delay) = how old the distance is when the decision is made.
ms.timing.why: You do not choose these, you measure them: the loop period is set by the sensor rate. What you DO choose is the speed: the faster you drive, the further the robot moves between two decisions and the older (in centimetres) its data is.
ms.timing.how: Motors are disabled for this test. Press Start: the robot reports its timing 12 times, then the normal profile is restored.
chk.ticks_range: {v} ticks per turn is implausible. Re-check that both wheels turned exactly once.
chk.ticks_lr: Left ({l}) and right ({r}) differ by more than 2 %: one wheel was turned more, or an encoder misses ticks.
chk.speed_range: Top speed {v} m/s is implausible: wheels in the air? battery charged?
chk.speed_lr: Left {l} and right {r} m/s differ by more than 10 %: a weak motor or gearbox.
chk.tau_range: Response time {v} s is implausible: was the target reachable?
chk.track: Track width {v} mm (wheel spacing {g} mm)? Re-check: count the turns again, and make sure the robot spun in place.
chk.tof_std: Sensor {n}: noise {v} mm is high. Is the target flat and not too far / too shiny?
chk.tof_drop: Sensor {n}: {v} % readings missing. Target out of range or at a bad angle?
chk.loop_slow: Loop period {v} ms is slow: the robot decides only a few times per second. Look for slow code in the loop.
chk.age_old: Reading age {v} ms is more than 3 loop periods: the data is old when used.

mz.intro: Test how robust maze-solving algorithms are on YOUR robot, with the same sensor, encoder and motor models as the corridor. Mazes are built wall by wall with small placement errors that add up, like a real hand-built maze. Left: the real maze. Right: what the robot believes (its own map from its sensors and encoders).
mz.edit: Edit walls (click a wall line, or a square in a block maze)
mz.thin: Thin walls (walls on the lines between cells)
mz.cell_hint: Your robot needs at least {n} mm to turn around in a cell.
mz.braid_hint: 0 = perfect maze (one path). More = loops, which defeat simple wall following.
mz.build_err_hint: Each wall is placed relative to its already-built neighbours, so errors add up across the maze. At the default the maze still looks perfect.
mz.algo_note: Algorithms get only sensor readings and encoders, like on the real robot: their map and position drift. The examples look around at each cell with the front sensor and centre between side walls while driving. Raise the noise to see them start failing.
mz.batch_p: Run the algorithm on many random mazes of these settings.
mz.batch_res: Found the exit in {ok} of {n} mazes
algo.wall_follower.desc: Keep the left hand on the wall: turn left if you can, else straight, else right, else back. No map needed; fails in mazes with loops around the exit.
algo.flood_fill.desc: Assume unknown walls are open, compute the distance of every cell to the exit, always move to the neighbour that is closest; recompute as walls are discovered (micromouse classic).
algo.dfs.desc: Depth-first exploration: go to an unvisited neighbour, otherwise go back the way you came, mapping everything on the way.
algo.custom.desc: Write create(ctx, kit) returning {step(obs) -> {left, right}}. See the comments in the template; kit.CellRobot does the driving and mapping for grid algorithms.

fw.intro: Tell us how your robot is wired and get a ready-to-flash Arduino sketch for the Measure page. The number, type and angle of the sensors come from the Sensors tab (the simulator uses the same list).
fw.board_note.uno: Uno / Nano: only D2 and D3 can call attachInterrupt; other pins need the PinChangeInterrupt library. PWM on D3, D5, D6, D9, D10, D11. I2C is A4 (SDA) / A5 (SCL). A6 / A7 exist on the Nano only and are analog inputs.
fw.board_note.mega: Mega: attachInterrupt on D2, D3, D18, D19, D20, D21 (D20 / D21 are also I2C). PWM on D2–D13 and D44–D46. I2C is D20 (SDA) / D21 (SCL).
fw.board_note.esp32: ESP32: every pin can interrupt and do PWM. GPIO 34–39 are input only (no pull-ups). GPIO 0, 2, 5, 12, 15 are strapping pins (read at reset). GPIO 6–11 belong to the flash chip. GPIO 1 / 3 are the USB serial.
fw.pin_table: Pins of this board and what they can do
fw.pin_table_note.uno: INT = attachInterrupt, PCINT = pin-change interrupt (PinChangeInterrupt library), PWM = analogWrite, ADC = analogRead.
fw.pin_table_note.mega: INT = attachInterrupt, PCINT = pin-change interrupt (PinChangeInterrupt library), PWM = analogWrite, ADC = analogRead.
fw.pin_table_note.esp32: INT = interrupt, PWM = analogWrite (LEDC), ADC = ADC1, ADC2 = analog only while Wi-Fi is off, strapping = read at reset.
fw.drv.in1_in2: Two inputs IN1 / IN2 (DRV8833, MX1508, L9110S, L298N with ENA jumper)
fw.drv.pwm_dir: PWM + DIR (DRV8838, DRV8835 phase/enable, Cytron MD10C)
fw.drv.en_in1_in2: EN + IN1 + IN2 (L298N with ENA wired, TB6612FNG)
fw.drv_note.in1_in2: Each motor has two inputs and both must be PWM pins: one gets the PWM, the other sets the direction (DRV8833 is this type, not PWM + DIR).
fw.drv_note.pwm_dir: One PWM pin sets the speed, one digital pin the direction.
fw.drv_note.en_in1_in2: EN gets the PWM, IN1 / IN2 the direction. TB6612FNG: PWMA = EN, AIN1 / AIN2 = IN1 / IN2, STBY optional (held HIGH).
fw.stop_note_in12: Also chooses the decay between PWM pulses: brake = slow decay (speed closer to proportional to PWM, recommended), coast = fast decay.
fw.stop_note_en: Only changes what happens at PWM 0.
fw.sign_note: If a wheel turns backwards when it should go forward, flip its sign (or swap its two motor wires).
fw.enc.single: Single channel (LM393 slotted disc, TT motors)
fw.enc_note.quadrature: Two channels 90° apart give the direction. ESP32: hardware pulse counter (PCNT). Uno / Mega: interrupts.
fw.enc_note.single: One channel: the sketch counts pulses and takes the sign from the commanded motor direction. When a wheel reverses it still turns the old way for a moment and those pulses are counted the wrong way: a few ticks of error at every reversal.
fw.enc_note.as5600: Absolute angle, 4096 steps per magnet turn; the sketch counts the turns. All AS5600 have address 0x36, so two need a TCA9548A multiplexer (or a second I2C bus on the ESP32).
fw.enc_note.none: Time-based mode: the wheels are driven without feedback. Steps of the Measure page that need encoders are disabled. The two motors never run at exactly the same speed, so the robot curves and turns drift.
fw.avr_x1: x1: channel A on D2 / D3 (attachInterrupt), B read for the direction
fw.avr_x4: x4: all four channels on interrupts (PinChangeInterrupt library where needed)
fw.ppr: Pulses per motor turn, per channel (PPR / lines)
fw.gear: Gear ratio (motor turns per wheel turn; 1 if the encoder is on the wheel)
fw.gear_magnet: Magnet turns per wheel turn (1 = magnet on the wheel axle)
fw.ticks_line: Ticks per wheel turn: {c} computed ({e} counted edges per pulse); the sketch starts with {u}. CAL TICKS on the Measure page measures the real value.
fw.ticks_low: Fewer than 100 ticks per turn: the sketch measures the wheel speed from the time between pulses.
fw.sensors_note: Add, remove, turn and move sensors on the Sensors tab.
fw.i2c_fixed: I2C is fixed on this board: SDA {sda}, SCL {scl}.
fw.suggest_note: Keeps the pins you chose that are valid, and gives every missing or invalid one a free pin that can do the job.

tut.s1.title: 1. Why PID?
tut.s1.body:
Four everyday problems:

  • A drone should hover at 10 m, but gravity and wind keep pushing it.
  • A self-balancing robot (two wheels) should stand upright, but every small push tips it over.
  • An air conditioner should keep the room at 22°, but someone opens a window.
  • A corridor robot should drive in the middle of a narrow corridor, parallel to the walls, but the walls are not perfect, the sensors are noisy and the motors are not identical.

All four are the same problem. There is an error e: the difference between what we want and what we measure. For our robot e is the distance to the left wall minus the distance to the right wall; it is 0 exactly in the middle and parallel. The question is always: how do we bring e to 0 and keep it there? That is the question PID answers.
tut.s2.title: 2. The definition
tut.s2.body:
We measure a quantity y(t) and want it to reach a target r(t). The error is the difference:

e(t) = r(t) − y(t)

For the corridor robot: target r = 0 (both distances equal), so e = dleft − dright. Move the robot in the demo and watch the sign of e.

From the error alone, the PID computes a command u(t), the sum of three terms:

u(t) = Kp·e(t) + Ki·∫0t e(τ) dτ + Kd·de/dt
tut.s2.body2:
The goal, formally: the error goes to 0 as time goes to infinity,

limt→∞ e(t) = 0  ⇔  ∀ε > 0 ∃T ∀t > T: |e(t)| < ε

In words: however small a band ε you pick, there is a moment T after which the error stays inside it. After every disturbance, the same again.

The robot's computer works in steps of Δt, so the integral becomes a sum and the derivative a difference:

u[k] = Kp·e[k] + Ki·Σj≤k e[j]·Δt + Kd·(e[k] − e[k−1]) / Δt
tut.s3.title: 3. Why correcting by the error alone is not enough
tut.s3.body:
The simplest idea: "the further I am from the centre, the harder I turn back". That is P alone. Watch what happens:

  1. The robot is 5 cm right of the centre. P turns it left, and it starts driving diagonally towards the centre.
  2. At the centre the error is 0, so P says "stop turning". But not turning is not driving straight: the robot is still pointing diagonally.
  3. So it passes the centre, P turns it back, and it overshoots again. Like a pendulum: at the lowest point it is fastest, so it swings through.

To stop at the centre the robot must see where the error is going, not only where it is now. That is exactly the job of D.

In the demo Kd starts at 0: the robot overshoots and keeps swinging. Raise Kd until it settles without overshooting.
tut.s3.demo: P alone overshoots. Add some Kd.
tut.s4.title: 4. The three terms
tut.s4.body:
• P, the present. A spring that pulls back with a force for every cm of error. A soft spring is lazy, a hard spring bounces.
  • D, the future. How fast the error is changing. If the robot is approaching the centre quickly, D straightens it before it arrives, so it reaches the centre parallel. Like a shock absorber: it reacts to speed, not to position.
  • I, the past. Error accumulated over time. Even a small error, if it does not go away, makes I push harder and harder.

When do you need I? When staying on target needs a constant push F (a drone against gravity, or a robot with one weaker wheel). With P alone, F has to come from Kp·e, so an error remains:

Kp·e = F  ⇒  e = F / Kp ≠ 0

The fix: I, which builds up F by itself (or add F directly to the command: feed-forward). A straight corridor needs no constant turning, so expect Ki to be small.

In the demo the right wheel is a bit weaker (wheel mismatch). With Ki = 0 the robot settles off-centre. Raise Ki and the offset disappears.
tut.s4.demo: A weak wheel leaves an offset. Ki removes it.
tut.s5.title: 5. PID on a corridor robot
tut.s5.body:
The error. The robot has two side distance sensors, one per wall, at 90° (straight at the wall) or 45° (diagonally forward). PID works with both: in the middle and parallel, both sensors see the same distance, so

e = dleft − dright

A positive error means the left wall is further away: the robot is near the right wall and must turn left.

The wheel commands. The PID gives one number, u. To turn, add it to one wheel and subtract it from the other:

vleft = base − u    vright = base + u

The average of the two wheels does not change (forward speed stays base), and the difference between them (2u) turns the robot.
tut.s5.demo: Move u and speed_frac. Watch for clipping.
tut.s5.body2:
A constant base speed. base is fixed once for the whole run, between the slowest speed a wheel can hold (vmin, below it the motor stalls) and the top speed:

base = vmin + speed_frac · (vmax − vmin)

For example speed_frac = 0.75: fast, and still room to steer.

Why not drive at top speed? Then base + u is above the maximum and the outer wheel is clipped: it cannot go faster, so the robot turns less than the PID asked for. For the same reason base cannot be vmin either: the inner wheel would drop below vmin and stall. 0.75 is only a starting point: if the robot still steers weakly, lower it; if there is plenty of room, raise it.

Another option: variable speed. Drive as fast as possible while keeping exactly enough room to turn: base = vmax − |u|. Full speed on the straights, slower exactly as much as needed in the turns. The price: the speed changes during the run.
tut.s6.title: 6. What happens when you change the gains
tut.s6.table:
ChangeWhat the robot does
Kp too smallLazy: drifts towards a wall and corrects late
Kp too largeWobbles around the centre, up to hitting a wall
Kd too small (or 0)P's swinging does not die out
Kd too largeCreeps to the centre slowly; nervous with noise
Ki too smallA small constant error stays (only if a constant push is needed)
Ki too largeSlow swinging and a big overshoot after a hold-up
tut.s6.demo: Distance from the centre while the robot drives (starts 5 cm off centre)
tut.s6.body:
With good gains the robot reaches 0 quickly and stays there. With Kp too large it wobbles around 0; with P alone the swinging even grows (because of the small delay between measurements). With Kd too large it gets there, but very slowly. Try the four buttons above, then move the sliders yourself.

Tuning by hand, in four steps:

  1. Start with Ki = 0 and Kd = 0.
  2. Raise Kp until the robot returns to the centre quickly (it will overshoot and wobble; that is fine at this step).
  3. Raise Kd until the wobbling calms down.
  4. Add a small Ki only if a constant offset remains.

Tip: log the error at every step and plot it like the graph above. Wobbling, overshoot or a constant offset are much easier to see on a graph than by eye.

Why there are no universal gains: the gains translate the error into a command, so they depend on the units, the speed, the sensors and the loop period. Gains from one robot at one speed will not work the same on another robot, or on the same robot at another speed.
tut.s7.title: 7. Two traps: windup and a noisy D
tut.s7.body:
Windup. When a wheel is already at full speed, or the robot is stuck, the error stays large and the integral keeps adding up. When the robot is released, the integral is huge and the robot overshoots hard to the other side. Example: hold the robot by hand 5 cm off centre for 5 seconds, then let go. With a large Ki and no limit it swings hard to the other side until the integral has unwound. The fix: clamp the integral to a fixed range, and reset it to 0 when the situation changes (for example a wall disappears).

A filter on D. D divides a difference by a small time step, so it amplifies noise: a 2 mm jump in one reading looks like a fast movement and jerks the wheels. The fix: average the derivative with the previous values. The price: D reacts a little later, so do not overdo it. alpha close to 1 = almost no filter; alpha close to 0 = a strong but slow filter.

The demo shows the turn command u with noisy sensors. Lower alpha and watch the command calm down.
tut.s7.demo: Noisy sensors: the D filter calms the command
tut.s8.title: 8. The inner PID: each wheel's speed
tut.s8.body:
The steering PID decides what speed each wheel should have, but a motor takes a voltage (PWM), and two motors never turn exactly alike for the same PWM. So each wheel has its own small PID: the error is the difference between the wanted speed and the speed the encoder measures, and the command is the PWM. It runs faster than the steering loop and only cares about the speed.

So the two loops share the work: the inner one makes sure the wheels do what was asked, the outer one cares about the direction.

Rule of thumb: the inner loop must be several times faster than the outer one. Otherwise the wheels do not reach their speed before the steering already asks for something else, and every correction arrives late.
tut.s9.title: Go deeper (optional)
tut.s9.summary: Does every set of gains settle? A short stability proof, and gains as times
tut.s9.body:
No. Some gains make the error swing forever, or grow, or settle at a value other than 0. A simple model of a robot in a corridor (sensors at 90°; at 45° the error also sees the angle, which only helps) shows when.

Definitions. y: the robot's sideways distance from the centre line (+ = left). θ: the angle between the robot and the corridor direction (small, + = turned left). v: forward speed (base, constant). W: wheel spacing. u: the PID command (wheels get base − u and base + u). c: a positive constant linking the error to the distance (e = −c·y).

Step 1: how the robot moves. A slightly rotated robot drifts sideways at v·θ; the angle changes with the wheel difference:

ẏ = v·sin θ ≈ v·θ,   θ̇ = (vright − vleft) / W = 2u / W  ⇒  ÿ = (2v / W)·u

Step 2: add a PD controller. Put u = Kpe + Kdė and e = −c·y into the equation:

ÿ + a·Kd·ẏ + a·Kp·y = 0,   a = 2vc / W > 0

Step 3: solve. Try y(t) = A·eλt:

λ² + a·Kd·λ + a·Kp = 0,   λ1 + λ2 = −a·Kd,   λ1·λ2 = a·Kp

y (and so e) goes to 0 if and only if both roots have a negative real part, which happens exactly when the sum is negative and the product positive: Kp > 0 and Kd > 0. With Kd = 0 the roots are purely imaginary and the robot swings forever: that is the failure of P alone from section 3.

In practice there are two more conditions:

  1. An upper limit. A real robot has delay, and the controller runs in steps, so gains that are too large make it swing (the red line in the graph of section 6), and even larger ones make the swinging grow. There is a window: large enough to correct, small enough not to swing.
  2. Without a constant push, or with I. PD settles on the target only if no constant push is needed. If one is needed (a weaker wheel, section 4), PD settles on an error that is not 0. Only I or feed-forward brings the limit to 0.

Gains as times. Dividing two gains gives a time, and that makes them easier to understand.

Kd/Kp: how far ahead D looks. For a short time τ, the error in τ seconds is the error now plus τ times its slope. Choose τ = Kd/Kp:

e(t + τ) ≈ e(t) + τ·ė(t),   Kpe + Kdė = Kp(e + (Kd/Kp)ė) ≈ Kp·e(t + Kd/Kp)

So P and D together act like P alone, but on the error expected Kd/Kp seconds from now. For example Kp = 0.6 and Kd = 0.4: the controller looks 0.67 s ahead.

Kp/Ki: how long I takes to catch up. With a constant error e, P pushes Kp·e at once and I adds Ki·e every second. After T seconds I pushes as much as P when Ki·e·T = Kp·e, so T = Kp/Ki.

own.intro: Three steps. Then the Tuner can measure your robot, and its numbers fit your code.
own.s1: Use the tabs below. Firmware: board, pins, encoder, motor driver. Sensors: where each sensor looks. Motor: speeds and timing. A pin is a numbered connection on the board. An encoder counts wheel turns in small steps (ticks). The motor driver is the chip that powers the motors.
own.s2: Press COPY PROMPT and paste it into your AI (ChatGPT, Claude, ...). Attach two things: your own robot code (all files), and the reference file (DOWNLOAD REFERENCE). The reference is the code the Tuner would write for this hardware, so your AI sees exactly what the Tuner expects.
own.copied: Prompt copied. Paste it into your AI.
own.copy_fail: Copy did not work. Open the preview, select the text and copy it.
own.prompt_note: The prompt holds your hardware and your current numbers. Change something below and it updates.
own.s3: Open the AI's code in the Arduino IDE (the free program that sends code to the board) and press Upload with the USB cable. Close the Arduino Serial Monitor, then press CONNECT here. For the tests where the robot drives, connect over Bluetooth instead (steps below).
own.compile_note: Robot Tuner does not compile code in the browser (the ESP32 tools are far too big for a web page). Always upload with the Arduino IDE.
own.cmd_ph: Type a command, e.g. STATUS or CAL DIR
own.nosupport: This browser cannot use USB serial. Use Chrome or Edge on a computer.
own.fail: Something fails? Open Troubleshooting. Or copy the exact error (from the Arduino IDE or from the box above) into your AI and ask it to fix the code.
own.next: When the robot answers, go on with Measure. Before you copy any gain into your code, read Using the Tuner's numbers in your own code.

nums.h1: Using the Tuner's numbers in your own code
nums.intro: The Tuner gives you numbers (gains). They only work if your code uses them the same way: same units, same loop, same timing. This page shows how.
nums.two_pid: A PID is a small controller. It looks at an error (wanted minus measured) and decides how hard to push. P pushes for the error now, I for the error that has added up, D for how fast the error changes.
nums.two_steer: Steering PID: walls → wheel speeds. Input: left distance minus right distance (metres). Output: how much faster the right wheel goes than the left (m/s).
nums.two_wheel: Wheel PID: makes each wheel reach its speed. Input: wanted minus measured wheel speed (encoder ticks per 10 ms). Output: PWM, the motor power (0 to 255).
nums.two_chain: The steering PID runs each time all sensors have a new reading. The wheel PID runs every 10 ms, faster, underneath it.
nums.units_note: Your current numbers. Each unit is taken from the code the simulator runs. "What 1.0 means" tells you how big one unit is.
nums.why_h: Why gains can't be copied between codes
nums.why_speed: We count encoder ticks per 10 ms. Some codes use percent of top speed instead. The same Kp then gives a different push. Example: the wheel should do 30 ticks per 10 ms and does 20.
nums.why_speed_pct: A percent code (top speed 43 ticks per 10 ms): error 10 ÷ 43 = 0.23. Kp 2 → 0.46 of full power = 0.46 × 255 = 117 PWM. Almost 6 times harder.
nums.why_ff: We first give the PWM that fits the wanted speed. This is called feedforward: a guess made before there is any error. The PID then only fixes small errors. Codes without it need much bigger PID gains. Other names for parts of it: min PWM, kick, jump start, deadband.
nums.why_delay: Some codes smooth the speed reading (average the last values). Smoothing makes the reading arrive late. Gains that work for us can then make their wheels shake. If your code smooths, set Speed smoothing in the Robot builder (Motor tab) to the same time constant and tune again.
nums.conv_note: Formulas, each with an example from your robot profile.
nums.c_mpt: Metres per tick = π × wheel diameter ÷ ticks per revolution = π × {d} mm ÷ {t} = {mpt} mm.
nums.c_tp: Ticks per period → m/s: m/s = ticks × metres per tick ÷ period. Example: {tp} ticks per {p} ms → {v} m/s.
nums.c_mps: m/s → ticks per period: ticks = m/s × period ÷ metres per tick. Example: {v} m/s → {tp} ticks per {p} ms.
nums.c_rpm: m/s → RPM (wheel turns per minute): RPM = m/s ÷ (π × diameter) × 60. Example: {v} m/s with a {d} mm wheel → {rpm} RPM.
nums.c_pct: m/s → percent of max: % = m/s ÷ max speed × 100. Example: {v} ÷ {vmax} m/s = {pct} %.
nums.c_gain: Wheel gain for a percent code (error as a fraction of top speed, output 0..1 instead of 0..255): Kp_new = Kp × ticks at top speed ÷ 255. Example: Kp {kp} × {tmax} ÷ 255 = {kpf}. Start PWM: {ff} ÷ 255 = {fff}. Ki, Kd and ff_gain the same way.
nums.c_period: Another loop period: r = new ÷ old. Kp ÷ r, Ki stays, Kd ÷ r², ff_gain ÷ r, start PWM stays. Example {p} ms → {p2} ms: Kp {kp} → {kp2}, Ki {ki} → {ki}, Kd {kd} → {kd2}, ff_gain {ff} → {ff2}.
nums.c_ki: Integral and derivative per second: we add the error once per period, without dt. If your code uses error × dt (seconds): Ki_new = Ki ÷ period = {ki} ÷ {p} ms = {kis}. If your D is per second: Kd_new = Kd × period = {kd} × {p} ms = {kds}.
nums.ticks_ab: A quadrature encoder has two signals, A and B, a quarter step apart. Each change of a signal is an edge. The order of the edges tells the direction.
nums.ab_alt: Signals A and B, and which edges x1, x2 and x4 count
nums.ticks_x: x1 counts the rising edges of A. x2 counts both edges of A. x4 counts every edge of A and B. The same wheel turn gives 4 times more ticks with x4 than with x1. So ticks per revolution depends on your code, not only on the encoder.
nums.ticks_hand: Don't trust the datasheet number: gear ratios are often rounded, and the decoding changes it. Turn the wheel once by hand while the robot counts: CAL TICKS on the Measure page.
nums.check_h: Checklist before you trust the numbers
nums.check_dir: Direction signs: send CAL DIR (wheels in the air). Both wheels turn forward and both counts go up.
nums.check_ticks: Ticks per revolution: measured with CAL TICKS, with the same decoding (x1/x2/x4) as your code.
nums.check_units: Units: your code measures speed in the same unit as the gain, or you converted the gain (above).
nums.check_period: Loop period: your wheel loop runs at the same period as the Tuner (Motor tab, wheel PID period), or you converted the gains.
nums.check_smooth: Smoothing: if your code smooths the speed reading, Speed smoothing in the Robot builder has the same time constant.

cmd.dir_h: Wheels in the air. Each wheel turns forward for a moment; both must turn forward and count up.
cmd.ticks_h: Then turn each wheel exactly one turn forward by hand.
cmd.end_h: Shows how many ticks one wheel turn gave.
cmd.maxspeed_h: Wheels in the air. Full power for 1 second.
cmd.vmin_h: Wheels in the air. Finds the slowest speed each wheel can hold.
cmd.ff_h: Wheels in the air. Steps the power up and measures the speed at each step.
cmd.step_h: Wheels in the air. Jumps to a speed and measures how fast the wheel gets there.
cmd.timed_h: For robots without encoders. Measure how far it drove yourself.
cmd.drive_h: On the floor. Drives this far by the encoders.
cmd.dist_h: Type the real distance it drove, in metres.
cmd.spin_h: On the floor. Spins this many turns by the encoders.
cmd.turns_h: Type how many turns it really made.
cmd.run_h: On the floor between two walls. Follows the walls with the PID for this many seconds.
cmd.tof_h: Takes readings from every sensor. Put a wall at a known distance to also get the error.
cmd.status_h: Last readings and how often the sensors update.
cmd.g_wheels: Wheels (lift the robot so the wheels spin freely)
cmd.dir_do: Lift the robot so both wheels hang free (a box or a cup under it).|Keep your hands away from the wheels.|Press Send and watch: the left wheel, then the right wheel turns for a moment.
cmd.dir_next: Both wheels must turn FORWARD and the result says OK. WRONG = flip the encoder sign (wheel turned forward) or the motor sign (wheel turned backward) in Firmware.
cmd.ticks_do: Put a pen or tape mark on each tyre, next to something fixed.|Press Send.|Turn the LEFT wheel forward by hand, slowly, exactly one full turn (mark back at the start).|Do the same with the RIGHT wheel.
cmd.ticks_next: Press "Done turning: show ticks". The number is your ticks per wheel turn.
cmd.end_do: Only after "Start counting ticks" and turning each wheel one full turn.
cmd.end_next: The robot prints the ticks of each wheel and a suggested value.
cmd.maxspeed_do: Lift the robot so both wheels hang free.|Hold it steady: the wheels run at full power for 1 second.
cmd.maxspeed_next: You get the top speed of each wheel in m/s.
cmd.vmin_do: Lift the robot so both wheels hang free.|Wait: each wheel slowly speeds up, forward then backward (about half a minute).
cmd.vmin_next: You get the slowest speed every wheel can hold.
cmd.ff_do: Lift the robot so both wheels hang free.|Wait: the power goes up step by step (about 15 seconds).
cmd.ff_next: You get the start PWM (ff_static) and PWM per speed (ff_gain).
cmd.step_do: Lift the robot so both wheels hang free.|The wheels jump to the speed in the box for 1.5 seconds.
cmd.step_next: You get how long the wheels need to reach the speed (rise time, tau).
cmd.timed_do: Connect over Bluetooth, unplug USB, robot on battery.|Put the robot on the floor with 2 m free in front. Mark where it starts.|Press Send: it drives at full power for the time in the box.
cmd.timed_next: Measure how far it went. Top speed = distance ÷ time.
cmd.drive_do: Connect over Bluetooth, unplug USB, robot on battery.|Put the robot on the floor with 1.5 m free in front. Mark the front of the robot.|Press Send: it drives the distance in the box by its encoders.
cmd.drive_next: Measure how far it really went, type it in the box of "I measured the distance" and press that button.
cmd.dist_do: Type the distance the robot REALLY drove (metres) in the box.
cmd.dist_next: The robot prints the wheel scale for each side (wscale).
cmd.spin_do: Connect over Bluetooth, unplug USB, robot on battery.|Put the robot on the floor in an open spot. Mark which way it points.|Press Send: it spins on the spot.
cmd.spin_next: Count the real turns (for example 4.75), type them in "I counted the turns" and press that button.
cmd.turns_do: Type how many turns the robot REALLY made in the box.
cmd.turns_next: The robot prints the effective track width.
cmd.run_do: Connect over Bluetooth, unplug USB, robot on battery.|Put the robot between two walls, in the middle, pointing along the corridor.|Keep STOP in reach.
cmd.run_next: It follows the walls for the time in the box and stops by itself. Press STOP to end it sooner.
cmd.tof_do: Put the robot still. Keep hands out of the sensors' view.|For the error too: put a flat wall at a known distance in front of each sensor and type that distance.
cmd.tof_next: You get the noise, the error (bias) and the dropouts of each sensor.
cmd.status_next: You get the last readings and how often the sensors deliver a new set.
cmd.motors_off_next: The motors stay off until "Motors on".
cmd.m_hand_h: Motors are off. You turn the wheels yourself.
cmd.m_air_h: The wheels spin. Lift the robot so they turn freely. It stays in place, so USB is fine.
cmd.m_floor_h: The robot drives on the floor on its battery, with NO cable. Connect over Bluetooth first (ESP32). No Bluetooth? Do not drive with the USB cable plugged in: skip this and type the value by hand on the Measure page.
cmd.floor_usb: These make the robot drive: connect over Bluetooth, robot on battery, no cable. No Bluetooth? Do not drive with the USB cable plugged in: skip this and type the value by hand on the Measure page.
cmd.ping_h: Sends PING; the robot answers PONG. The site also does this by itself every 3 seconds.
cmd.ping_next: The status next to CONNECT turns green when the robot answers.
link.off_h: Press CONNECT and pick the robot's port.
link.waiting: … Port open, waiting for the robot
link.waiting_h: The port is open. Waiting for the first answer (the board may be restarting).
link.ok_h: The robot answered PING in the last few seconds: commands will reach it.
link.foreign: ◐ Something answers, but not to PING
link.foreign_h: Text arrives, but no PONG. The robot runs an older sketch or code without the Robot Tuner commands: upload the newest code.
link.silent_h: The port is open but nothing comes back. Check: right port, robot powered, the Robot Tuner code uploaded, baud 115200, Arduino Serial Monitor closed.
fw.bt_note: The robot answers over USB and Bluetooth at the same time, so it can drive on the floor without a cable. Your PC keeps its WiFi and internet. Pair the PC with the robot once in the Bluetooth settings, then press CONNECT and pick the Bluetooth port. Only the classic ESP32 has it: switch it off for ESP32-S3, C3 or C6.
bt.steps: Upload the code once with the USB cable (Bluetooth on in Robot builder → Firmware).|Unplug USB and power the robot from its battery.|On the PC: Bluetooth settings → Add device → pick "{name}". Windows then creates a COM port ("Standard Serial over Bluetooth link"); on a Mac it appears as /dev/cu.{name}.|Press CONNECT here and pick that port. When the status turns green, the robot answers.
bt.no_wifi: Why not WiFi? This site runs over https, and browsers do not let https pages talk to a robot's plain WiFi address. Bluetooth shows up as a normal serial port, and your PC stays on its WiFi.
